original_baseline.name: Original Baseline Query
original_baseline.description: Original query with full telemetry projection (11 usage columns + 6 event columns).

candidate_a.name: Candidate A: Projection Reduction
candidate_a.description: Minimal leaf projection: 6 usage columns + 4 event columns. Dropped non-essential fields.

candidate_b.name: Candidate B: Source-Scan Reduction
candidate_b.description: Consolidated instance_events CTE to prevent multiple table references, plus minimal leaf projection.

candidate_c.name: Candidate C: Bounded Pilot Scope
candidate_c.description: Explicit bounded collection ID filter (5 jobs) and 1-hour micro-horizon (3.6e9 us). Tests unpartitioned row pruning.

candidate_d.name: Candidate D: Alternative Access Strategy
candidate_d.description: Alternative access strategy using collection_events (20.8M rows) for job-level failure prediction.

key_empirical_findings: 1. In Google Borg ClusterData 2019, instance_usage has 7,575,500,668 rows with no partitioning or clustering.
2. In BigQuery columnar storage, every 8-byte column in instance_usage scans exactly 60,604,005,344 bytes (56.44 GiB / 60.6 GB).
3. Any query referencing instance_usage scans at least 60.6 GB per column, making a 21.0 GB cap physically impossible on the public table.
4. Candidates A, B, and C (which retain container telemetry) all scan 418,578,205,568 bytes (418.58 GB, $2.38 USD), exceeding the budget by 19.0x.
5. Candidate C proves that row filters (WHERE collection_id IN (...) or WHERE time <= ...) yield 0% scan reduction on unclustered/unpartitioned tables.

6. Candidate D (alternative access strategy via collection_events) scans 2,520,117,308 bytes (2.52 GB, $0.014 USD), satisfying budget limits but shifting scope from container telemetry to job-level lifecycle transitions.
